name: Oui-Spy
firmware_note: Six modes in one image, picked from a boot menu served over the device's own Wi-Fi AP: BLE watchlist detector, RSSI foxhunter, Flock Safety camera sniffer, Wi-Fi PCAP, drone Remote ID, BLE sniffer.
price_note: $85 assembled from colonelpanic.tech. The bare 2-PCB set is $25 and you add your own $7.49 Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3. Wearable variants running the same firmware: patch $75, earring set $60.
skill_note: Flash from a web page, join its Wi-Fi AP, pick a mode from a menu. No CLI needed for normal use.
build_note: Ships assembled. Firmware updates via a Web Serial page in Chrome/Edge/Opera, or a bundled Python flasher. No toolchain required.
summary: A passive 2.4 GHz surveillance-detection scanner: a Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 on a pair of art PCBs with a piezo buzzer and an RGB LED. It listens for BLE and Wi-Fi signatures belonging to surveillance hardware - Flock Safety ALPR cameras, Axon/Taser, Ring, DJI/Parrot/Skydio drones, Meta Ray-Bans - and beeps when it matches one. The name is a pun on OUI, the vendor prefix in a MAC address, which is what most of its matching is built on.
honest_take: It is a $7.49 XIAO ESP32-S3 with a buzzer and an LED on two art PCBs, sold for $85 - you are buying the curated signature lists, the boot-menu firmware and the silkscreen, not the silicon. It only hears 2.4 GHz, so it will miss any camera that talks over LTE and does not also beacon Wi-Fi or BLE. And 'detection' means matching MAC OUI prefixes, BLE company IDs and service UUIDs against a hand-maintained list, which any vendor defeats by rotating MACs - the README says exactly that about Meta's Ray-Bans, which is why those get a separate composite rule instead.
best_for: Finding Flock Safety ALPR cameras on a drive or walk
Direction-finding a specific BLE device by ear
Passive drone Remote ID monitoring
Learning what BLE and Wi-Fi actually leak
not_for: Anything on 5 GHz, sub-GHz, or cellular
Detecting hardware that is not already on a published signature list
Wardriving with GPS - there is no GPS on the board
Any offensive use - the shipped modes only listen

radios.note: 2.4 GHz 802.11b/g/n plus Bluetooth LE 5. No 5 GHz, no sub-GHz, no nRF24, no cellular.

PWM piezo buzzer driven from a dedicated FreeRTOS task

ble_sniff.note: Passive advertising capture on channels 37/38/39, rolling 2 MB PCAP in PSRAM (LINKTYPE_BLUETOOTH_LE_LL_WITH_PHDR, 256), downloadable from the web UI.

ble_advertise.note: Shipped modes are receive-only. The same author publishes a separate Remote-ID-Spoofer build that does transmit - different firmware, different repo.

wifi_scan_5.note: ESP32-S3 radio is 2.4 GHz only. There is no 5 GHz path on this hardware.

wifi_monitor_mode.note: esp_wifi promiscuous mode; in Flock-You mode the AP is disabled so the radio is dedicated to sniffing.

wifi_probe_sniff.note: Used for the DeFlockJoplin wildcard-probe signature: type=0 subtype=4 with a zero-length SSID IE and a known OUI in addr2.

packet_capture.note: 802.11 with radiotap, linktype 127, 2 MB rolling session buffer in PSRAM, one-click download plus per-frame CSV snapshot.

wifi_ap_mode.note: Hosts a config/dashboard AP (default oui-spy / ouispy123 at 192.168.4.1). Disabled in the sniffing-only modes so the radio is not shared.

web_ui.note: Per-mode dashboards with live tables, vendor colouring, CSV snapshot and PCAP download.

detect_surveillance_cam.note: Flock Safety specifically. Matches a 39-entry OUI list on addr2 (transmitter side) and addr1 (receiver side, catching STAs that only appear as a destination during burst-sleep windows), plus a wildcard-probe signature. Technique credited to @NitekryDPaul.

detect_drone.note: FAA Remote ID / ASTM F3411 (Open Drone ID) over Wi-Fi beacons and BLE. Parses Basic ID, Location, Authentication, Self-ID, System and Operator ID, so it reads the drone's own lat/lon, altitude, speed and heading.

detect_generic_ble.note: Curated vendor table: Ring, Axon (OUI 00:25:DF, company ID 0x034D, service UUID 0xFC81), Flock Safety, DJI, Parrot, Skydio, and a Meta/Luxottica composite rule (company ID 0x0D53 plus service UUID 0xFD5F, or a Ray-Ban/Wayfarer/Oakley Meta local name).

detect_generic_wifi.note: Same OUI table applied to 802.11 frames in the PCAP and Flock-You modes.

gps.note: No onboard GPS. In the Flock-You workflow position comes from the host running the companion Flask dashboard; drone positions come from the drone's own Remote ID telemetry.

sd_logging.note: Detections persist to internal SPIFFS with a CRC envelope. PCAPs live in PSRAM until downloaded. No card slot.

standalone_untethered.note: Runs headless with buzzer and LED alerts, but no battery is listed - you power it from USB-C or a power bank.

legal.notes: As shipped it only receives, which is legal in nearly every jurisdiction, and detecting police or ALPR hardware is not itself an offence in the US. The same author separately publishes a Remote-ID-Spoofer build that transmits fake drone Remote ID - that is a different firmware, and transmitting it is illegal in the US and EU. Check your local law before relying on any of this.

firmware_note: Ships blank for legal reasons; you flash GhostESP to both chips from the browser. GhostESP Revival is the actively-maintained GPL-3.0 fork of Spooky's archived Ghost ESP.
price_note: $219.99 on Tindie, in stock 2026-09-06. EUR209 ex-VAT direct from wiredhatters.com. Board, case and two dual-band antennas only: the 1S LiPo (vendor asks for 5000 mAh+ with BMS), the external GPS antenna and the microSD are all extra, so a working unit lands nearer $250-280. The ~$277 figure on some listings appears to be an older or bundled price.
skill_note: Two chips to flash separately, no firmware pre-installed, and you must source and fit your own battery before it leaves the desk.
build_note: Assembled board in a 3D-printed PLA case. You flash GhostESP to the ESP32-C5 and the ESP32-S3 separately via the web flasher, then add a battery and card.
summary: The most hardware-dense ESP32 handheld in this batch: an ESP32-C5 and an ESP32-S3 on one board, linked over UART, both running GhostESP. The C5 drives the colour touchscreen and provides the only dual-band (2.4 + 5 GHz) Wi-Fi radio; the S3 handles BLE, NFC, IR, wired Ethernet, USB host and GPS. It is aimed at people who want one device that covers Wi-Fi, BLE, NFC, IR and wired network work without carrying a bag of dongles.
honest_take: The 'dual-SoC' is two independent GhostESP nodes talking over a UART, not shared processing - and the C5 is simultaneously the display driver and the only 5 GHz radio, so it is doing both jobs at once. The 5 GHz itself is real and unusually well evidenced: GhostESP's changelog has entries for fixing 5 GHz channel discovery above UNII-1, AP-aware 5 GHz hopping, 5 GHz HT40 deauth tuning and role-split wardriving. What you do not get for $220 is sub-GHz - there is no CC1101 anywhere on this board, so a $49 LilyGo T-Embed CC1101 will open your garage and this will not - plus you supply the battery, the card and the GPS antenna, and the firmware doing all the work is free and runs on a $12.58 dongle.

One device covering Wi-Fi + BLE + NFC + IR + wired Ethernet

summary: A passive dual-radio counter-surveillance logger from the German vendor NetzSec. An ESP32-S3 runs the application and the BLE radio while a dedicated ESP32-C5 co-processor sweeps 2.4 and 5 GHz Wi-Fi, so both bands and BLE are captured in parallel rather than time-sliced. It classifies BLE trackers and beacons, flags follow-me devices and privacy leaks, and logs to microSD. It has no attack modes at all.
honest_take: 'ZeroTrace' is a whole product family, not one device - EUR19.85 BadUSB kits, a EUR34.85 USB-A HID stick, a EUR54.85 USB logger and this EUR129.85 scanner - and several completely unrelated projects share the name (a Tor-routing bash script, an AI dork generator, an Intel SGX ORAM research paper), so establish which one you are actually looking at. The 5 GHz here is real silicon, a dedicated ESP32-C5, but the firmware is closed, there is no source, no teardown and no independent review anywhere, so every capability claim is the vendor's word and nothing more. It is also purely receive-only: no deauth, no injection, no attack modes, which is a design decision rather than a limitation but does mean it is not a substitute for a Ghost ESP or Bruce device.

An ESP32-WROOM-UE drives a touchscreen running ESP32 Marauder directly, while an ESP32-WROVER is controlled by the Flipper through its GPIO header. honest_take: $173 buys two 2.4 GHz-only ESP32 modules and a GPS on one board. The two chips do not cooperate - one drives the screen, one answers the Flipper, and the single GPS is switched between them, so you get one working Marauder at a time, not two. Roughly 40 modules spanning Wi-Fi, BLE, 2.4 GHz nRF24, sub-GHz via CC1101 and NFC via PN532 or Chameleon Ultra, plus detection features and named CVE modules. honest_take: Almost every write-up calls HaleHound open source. It is not. The repo holds a README and a proprietary licence and zero lines of code, the binaries come only from the author's own web flasher (the GitHub releases carry no assets), and the licence explicitly forbids redistributing, modifying or selling them - while the thing itself is a derivative of CiferTech's MIT-licensed ESP32-DIV. On the hardware side, 'broadband jamming' means an nRF24L01+PA+LNA spraying 2.4 GHz at +20 dBm rather than any real wideband jammer, the documented CC1101 wiring only covers 300-439 MHz so it will not touch 868 or 915 MHz gear, and no ESP32-WROOM-32 build can ever do BadUSB.

price_note: $87.35 list at LILYGO, sold out across all variants on 2026-09-06. Third-party sellers were asking $100-101 including shipping. An nRF24L01 2.4 GHz shield is sold separately.
skill_note: Multiple competing firmwares (Meshtastic, MeshCore, Bruce) with different flashing routes, and Bruce's support here is partial.
build_note: Assembled handheld with keyboard, battery and case. You choose and flash a firmware; nothing security-related is pre-installed.
summary: A finished ESP32-S3 handheld with a QWERTY keyboard, a 2.33-inch wide display, an SX1262 LoRa radio, u-blox GNSS, NFC, an audio codec and an AI motion IMU. It is designed as an off-grid mesh communicator - Meshtastic and MeshCore are its real ecosystems - and Bruce will run on it, which is why it turns up in security-gadget comparisons.
honest_take: This is a LoRa mesh communicator that Bruce happens to run on, not a security tool that happens to have LoRa. Bruce's own device table puts it in the limited-support tier, and the sub-GHz radio is an SX1262 fixed to one band by SKU - it is not a CC1101 and it will not sweep 300-928 MHz or replay a 433 MHz garage remote unless you bought that variant, and Bruce's sub-GHz tooling is written around the CC1101 anyway. At $87 and sold out, you are paying for the GNSS, the keyboard, the audio codec and the IMU, none of which do anything for wireless attacks. If you want an ESP32-S3 handheld for RF work, the T-Embed CC1101 is $49 and has the right radio.

name: LilyGo T-Embed CC1101
firmware_note: Bruce's best-supported LilyGo target - the device table gives it full feature coverage including the built-in CC1101 and its antenna switch. GhostESP and CapibaraZero also build for it.
price_note: $49.38 for the standard board at LILYGO; the T-Embed CC1101 Plus, which is the same board plus a bundled nRF24L01 module, runs about $55-59. Some regional warehouse variants were showing out of stock on 2026-09-06.
skill_note: Flash Bruce from a browser and everything works from a rotary-encoder menu. No soldering, no add-on modules, no pin conflicts.
build_note: Finished device with a case, battery and antenna switch. Flashing Bruce takes a few minutes from a web flasher.
summary: The strongest ready-made Flipper Zero alternative in this batch: an ESP32-S3 handheld with a genuine CC1101 sub-GHz transceiver covering 300-928 MHz, a PN532 NFC reader, IR transmit and receive, a 1.9-inch colour screen and a rotary encoder, all onboard for about $49. Running Bruce it covers sub-GHz, NFC, IR, Wi-Fi, BLE and BadUSB from one menu.
honest_take: This is the one device here where the hardware genuinely earns the price - a real CC1101 across all three sub-GHz bands, a real PN532, real IR TX and RX, no soldering, no add-on modules, nothing shared with the display bus. Two things to know before buying. Several retail listings claim '125/134 kHz LF' RFID support; that is wrong - the PN532 is 13.56 MHz only, so this cannot read or clone an HID Prox or EM4100 badge, which is the single most common misconception about it. And it has no more rolling-code magic than a Flipper: it replays fixed codes and brute-forces static remotes, and that is the end of it.

Deauth, evil portals, BadUSB and card cloning each carry their own separate exposure. Owning the device is legal; a good deal of what it can do is not. Check your local law.

name: LilyGo T-Watch S3
firmware_note: GhostESP has a dedicated S3TWatch target with its own partition table, DRV2605 haptic feedback, IR support and a 4 MB virtual storage volume standing in for the absent SD card. Bruce also supports it, in its limited-feature tier.
price_note: $42.98 at LILYGO, sold out on 2026-09-06. The T-Watch S3 Plus, which adds GPS and a larger battery, is a separate and more expensive product.
skill_note: Flashing is easy; driving a menu system designed for larger screens on a 1.54-inch watch face is not.
build_note: Finished smartwatch with battery, case and strap. Flash GhostESP or Bruce from a browser.
summary: An open smartwatch built on an ESP32-S3, with a 1.54-inch capacitive touchscreen, an SX1262 LoRa radio, an IR LED, haptics, a microphone and speaker, and an AXP2101 power management IC. Flashed with GhostESP or Bruce it becomes a wrist-worn 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and BLE tool - the only genuinely wearable device in this batch.
honest_take: The reason to pick this over any other ESP32-S3 is that it looks like a watch, which matters for a physical assessment and for nothing else. Everything it does, a $12.58 T-Dongle-C5 does better: there is no SD card at all - GhostESP fakes a 4 MB internal volume, so handshake captures are measured in minutes rather than hours - no GPS, no CC1101, 2.4 GHz only, and a 1.54-inch screen driving menus built for bigger displays. LILYGO does not publish the battery capacity, which for a continuous-scan workload is the one number that actually matters. And it was sold out when checked.
